title: Is Waiting An Effective Strategy When Students Talk During A Lesson nts-talk-during-a-lesson/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin evaluates the common practice of pausing a lesson and waiting for talking students to quiet down, concluding that on its own it loses effectiveness over time — what takes seconds in September can take a minute by November and stop working entirely by January. His fix is pairing the wait with a clear, follow-up response that splits into two modes depending on scale. When only a handful of students are talking, waiting should be followed immediately by a specific consequence for each named student, which reinforces the sanctity of the lesson without further comment. When a larger portion of the class is talking, the teacher should instead cancel the lesson and fully reteach expectations, since large-scale disruption signals either unclear initial teaching or inconsistent enforcement. He notes the situation is almost always one or the other — a few students or most of the class — never something in between, framing that binary as key to selecting the correct response.
points: Waiting for talking students to quiet down loses effectiveness over time if not paired with a clear consequence.
When just a few students are talking, follow the wait with a specific, named consequence for each of them.
When most of the class is talking, cancel the lesson and fully reteach expectations rather than issuing individual consequences.
Large-scale disruption signals the teacher either wasn't clear enough in initial teaching or hasn't been consistently enforcing the plan.
The scale of talking during a lesson is almost always either a small few or most of the class, rarely something in between.
quotes: While it’s true that the strategy can help get wayward students back on track, it does little to ensure that it doesn’t happen again.
What may take just a few seconds of waiting in September takes nearly a minute in November. By January, it may not work at all.
The key is to pair the strategy with a clear and direct response.
John, Karla, Anthony, and Abigail, you each have a warning for breaking rule number two.
If, however, more than a few students are talking during your lesson, then it’s a sign that you’re either on the cusp of losing control of your class or you’re already there.
Because, either you weren't clear and detailed enough when you first taught and modeled how you want them to behave during lessons or you haven't been consistently holding them accountable.
More than a few, however, is on you, and a sign you must reteach and recommit.
